"And one more thing," said Yamini ma'am, the hostel warden, tapping the notice board. "Vaibhav, the terrace is locked for a reason. And you are not to hang around with the Class 12 boys who go up there. Understood?"
Everyone turned to look. Vaibhav's ears went hot. He hadn't even thought about the terrace before tonight.
At lights-out he lay staring at the ceiling fan. Who was she to pick his friends? Just before midnight he slipped out, found the Class 12 boys by the stairwell, and went up to the terrace edge with them. The wind was cold and the drop behind the low wall was dark.
He didn't enjoy it much. But he had gone, and that felt like the whole point.

qa.q: What did Yamini ma'am say about the terrace?
qa.a: She said the terrace is locked for a reason.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav go to the terrace even though he didn't enjoy it much?
qa.a: Being singled out and told whom to avoid made him feel his freedom was being taken, so going felt like proof that he still decided for himself.

qa.q: What might the warden try instead of a public order?
qa.a: Talk to Vaibhav privately, explain the real danger of the terrace, and let him help decide how the boys can spend time together safely.

qa.q: How might Yamini ma'am feel if she learned where Vaibhav went?
qa.a: She would likely feel frightened and frustrated, since her warning was meant to keep him safe and instead seemed to push him toward the danger.

grounding: It shows a teenage boy who is publicly told what to avoid doing the opposite, the pressure making a risky place more tempting.

Dear Chaitanya bhaiya,
You're the only one who won't lecture me, so I'm writing to you. Last month Amma saw Lakshya's messages on my phone and said I'm not allowed to talk to him again. Not "be careful", just "no, finished". She even changed the wifi password.
Honestly, before that I barely knew him. After that I messaged him every night from my friend's phone. Last Saturday he asked me to come and watch bike races on the ring road at midnight, and I said yes before I even thought. In the end I didn't go because it rained. I was almost relieved.
I don't even like bikes. I think I just hated being told. Is that stupid?
Your cousin brother,
Pradeep

qa.a: Amma changed the wifi password.

qa.q: Why was Pradeep almost relieved when it rained?
qa.a: Part of Pradeep never wanted to go to the midnight races; saying yes was mostly a way to push back against being told "no, finished".

qa.q: What would you advise Pradeep now?
qa.a: Talk to Amma at a calm moment, tell her honestly about the race invite, and ask for rules with reasons instead of a total ban; staying away from midnight races can be Pradeep's own choice.

qa.q: How might Amma see the secret messaging if she found out?
qa.a: She would probably feel hurt and more scared, since her ban was meant to protect Pradeep and instead led to secrecy and a risky invite.

Aadhya, you asked why I, Yash, the careful one, did the quarry thing. Okay. Papa heard about our quarry swim plan from someone's mum and just exploded. "You will not go. You will not see Ronit. You will be home by six every day this month." He said it in front of my little sister, like I was eight.
And something in me went: fine, watch me. I don't even swim that well. But that Sunday I told them I had extra class and went with Ronit. The water was freezing and so deep I couldn't see my own feet. I stayed near the edge the whole time, scared, pretending I wasn't.
Nothing happened. But I keep thinking about it. I went because of Papa, not because I wanted to.

qa.a: Yash told them there was extra class, and went with Ronit to the quarry.

qa.q: What does "fine, watch me" show about how Yash felt?
qa.a: Yash felt controlled and embarrassed at being ordered around in front of family, and doing the opposite felt like taking back the freedom to decide.

qa.q: What could Yash do the next time a strict order sparks the urge to rebel?
qa.a: Pause and ask whether the risky thing is actually wanted, then talk to Papa about the rule later instead of proving a point in deep water.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had explained his worry calmly instead of exploding?
qa.a: Yash would have had less to push against and could have heard the real fear about deep water, so the quarry would have felt much less tempting.

grounding: It shows a teenager who, told firmly what to do and whom to avoid, does the opposite, with the pressure making a risky swim more tempting.

Monday: Mahima found the gaming café receipt in Deepak's school bag. "You will never set foot in that place again. Do you hear me?" Deepak, fifteen, said nothing and went to his room. He hadn't even planned to go back; the games there were old.
Wednesday: He told his mother he had extra maths class and went to the café straight from school. He stayed till eight, not really enjoying it, glancing at the door every few minutes. When two older boys invited him to ride along to the highway at night, he almost said yes.
Saturday: Mahima sat on the edge of his bed. "I was scared, so I shouted. Here's what actually worries me: the late nights and those older boys. Can we work something out together?" Deepak stared at the floor for a long time. Then he said, "Friday afternoons at Sameer's house instead?"

passage: When I was fifteen, Appa found out I'd been talking to Vasudha every evening after tuition and said, very loudly, that it had to stop. No reasons, just "I don't want to hear her name in this house." I'm Jomon, and before that day, Vasudha was just a friend from maths class. After that day she became the most important person in my life. I called her from the terrace. I left early for tuition to walk with her. Every rule Appa added made me more determined. It wasn't until Amma sat me down, much later, and asked what I actually felt about Vasudha that I realised I didn't know. The ban had done all my feeling for me.

Counsellor's note, Thursday.
On Monday the principal announced in assembly, very sternly, that anyone seen near the old quarry would be suspended. Until then, I don't think Omkar had ever thought about the quarry. By Wednesday, he and Karthik had cycled there after school and climbed down to the water's edge. A shopkeeper saw them and called the school. In my room today, Omkar said, arms folded, "Nobody tells me where I can go." When I asked what he'd found there, he admitted the rocks were loose and he had slipped once. I didn't lecture. I explained why the quarry is dangerous and asked what would make it less tempting. He shrugged. "If they'd just said why." I called both boys' parents today, and asked the principal to explain the reasons at Friday's assembly.

qa.q: Who saw Omkar and Karthik at the quarry?
qa.a: A shopkeeper saw them and called the school.

qa.q: What does 'Nobody tells me where I can go' suggest about Omkar's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Omkar felt controlled and defiant, so the stern ban made the quarry tempting as a way to protect his freedom.

qa.q: What did the counsellor do, and why is it a better approach?
qa.a: The counsellor explained the danger instead of lecturing, called both boys' parents that day, and asked the principal to explain the reasons, which lowers the urge to rebel and keeps them safer.

qa.q: How might Karthik's parents feel getting the counsellor's call?
qa.a: They would likely feel alarmed about the loose rocks and grateful to know the same day.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose interest in a dangerous place was sparked by a stern ban, and a counsellor responding with reasons and protective steps.

In the kasba, everyone knew the old dam wall was off limits. Suraj's father had told him flatly at breakfast: "Don't go near the dam with those older boys. That's final."

By afternoon Suraj was walking toward the dam with his cousin Pooja, his chappals slapping the dust.

"You weren't even interested yesterday," Pooja said.

"He can't decide everything," Suraj muttered.

At the wall, the older boys were daring each other to walk the narrow edge. Suraj's stomach dropped. The water below was fast and brown.

Pooja grabbed his sleeve. "Come. Now." They walked home, and Pooja told his mother what the boys were doing. His mother called the sarpanch that evening, and a watchman was posted by the wall.

qa.q: What were the older boys daring each other to do?

qa.a: Suraj felt resentful at his father's flat order, and going felt like protecting his own freedom, not because he really wanted to go.

Before that night, Siddiq had thought Marek was a bit much: too loud, always on his skateboard, someone to nod at. Now, suddenly, Marek felt important.
The next afternoon Siddiq skipped chess club and went to the skate park. He didn't even like skating much. He just liked that it was his choice.
Marek tossed him a board. "Your dad let you out?"
"I let me out," Siddiq said, and his heart thumped with something between excitement and guilt.
He fell four times, scraped his elbow, and got home late with a story about the library. The lie felt heavier than the board.

At the boys' hostel, the new warden pasted a notice on every door: NO CRICKET IN THE CORRIDOR. NO EXCEPTIONS. VIOLATORS WILL BE REPORTED.
Tushar hadn't played corridor cricket since Class 8. It was cramped and boring. But that night he found an old tennis ball and knocked on Tarun's door.
"Corridor. Now."
"You hate corridor cricket."
"I hate being told in capital letters."
They played for fifteen minutes, whispering and giggling, until a ball smashed the glass case of the fire extinguisher. The warden came out in his vest.
In the office, the warden asked, "Why? You never played before."
Tushar looked at the floor. "Because the notice said I couldn't."
The warden sat back, surprised. "So if I'd explained that those glass cases break easily, you'd have left it alone?"
"Probably," Tushar admitted.

qa.q: What did the warden's notice say?
qa.a: It said: NO CRICKET IN THE CORRIDOR. NO EXCEPTIONS. VIOLATORS WILL BE REPORTED.

qa.q: Why did Tushar want to play corridor cricket that night?
qa.a: Tushar felt irritated at being ordered in capital letters and wanted to prove his freedom, even though he found the game boring.

qa.q: What could the warden do differently next time?
qa.a: Explain the reason, like the fragile glass cases, instead of issuing a harsh order, so students have less reason to push back.

qa.q: How does the warden react to Tushar's answer?
qa.a: The warden is surprised, and starts to see that explaining might work better than capital letters.
